name: Basque
variety: Standard Basque (Euskara Batua) in a central, Gipuzkoan or High Navarrese type of pronunciation without /h/; the pitch-accent systems of Northern Bizkaian (Lekeitio, Gernika, Getxo) and of Goizueta are described in the tone section
sources: Hualde, José Ignacio (1991). Basque Phonology. London: Routledge.
Hualde, José Ignacio and Ortiz de Urbina, Jon (eds.) (2003). A Grammar of Basque. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Hualde, José Ignacio (1999). Basque accentuation. In van der Hulst (ed.), Word Prosodic Systems in the Languages of Europe. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.

Hualde, José Ignacio; Elordieta, Gorka; Gaminde, Iñaki; Smiljanić, Rajka (2002). From pitch-accent to stress-accent in Basque. In Gussenhoven and Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Hualde, José Ignacio; Lujanbio, Oihana; Torreira, Francisco (2008). Lexical tone and stress in Goizueta Basque. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 38(1), 1-24.
Hualde, José Ignacio; Lujanbio, Oihana; Zubiri, Juan Joxe (2010). Goizueta Basque. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 40(1), 113-127.
Elordieta, Gorka and Hualde, José Ignacio (2014). Intonation in Basque. In Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology II. Oxford University Press.
Euskaltzaindia (1998). Euskara batuaren ahoskera zaindua (rule 87 of the Academy of the Basque Language).
Trask, R. L. (1997). The History of Basque. London: Routledge.
contrasts: three sibilant places, each with a fricative and an affricate: laminal (tongue blade) alveolar /s̻ ts̻/ written z, tz; apical (tongue tip) alveolar /s̺ ts̺/ written s, ts; and prepalatal /ʃ tʃ/ written x, tx (zu 'you' versus su 'fire'; hotz 'cold' versus hots 'noise'; atzo 'yesterday' versus atso 'old woman')
fricative versus affricate sibilant between vowels and at the end of a word (oso 'very' versus otso 'wolf'); apical versus laminal fricative also between vowels (hasi 'begin' versus hazi 'grow')
tap /ɾ/ versus trill /r/ between vowels (ere 'also' versus erre 'burn')
five vowels without length or nasality (the eastern dialect of Zuberoa adds /y/ and nasal vowels)
palatal consonants /ɲ ʎ c ɟ ʃ tʃ/, used also to form affectionate or diminutive variants of words (tt, dd, x in place of t, d, z)
voiced versus voiceless stops; northern dialects add aspirated stops and /h/
accent: position of the accent in most dialects; accented versus unaccented words in the pitch-accent dialects
allophony: /b d ɡ/ are approximants [β ð ɣ] between vowels and after most consonants, stops after pause and nasals (and /d/ after /l/), as in Spanish
after /n l r/ only affricates occur, not fricatives (pentsatu, beltz, bertso), and sibilants are voiced before a voiced consonant (esne [ez̺ne])

in Bizkaia and much of Gipuzkoa the apical and laminal series have merged: the fricatives as apical [s̺], the affricates as laminal [ts̻]; the standard and the central and eastern dialects keep them apart
/n l/ (in the west also /t/) become palatal after /i/ or a glide [j] before a vowel: mina [miɲa], mutila [mutiʎa], baina [baɲa]; general in western and central speech and tolerated by the norm

written j has different values by region: [x] in Gipuzkoa and widely in the south, [j] in the north and in the recommended standard pronunciation, a palatal stop or fricative in parts of Bizkaia, [ʒ] in Zuberoa
written h is silent in the south; the northern dialects pronounce [h] and have aspirated stops
after the negative particle ez, initial voiced stops are devoiced and z plus z gives an affricate (ez da [es̻ta], ez dut [es̻tut], ez zen [ets̻en])
the rhotic contrast exists only between vowels; the trill is used at the start of a syllable after a consonant and in the coda; native words do not begin with r
stops are voiceless unaspirated in the south
syllable_structure: (C)V(G)(C)(C), with onset clusters of stop or f plus liquid in loanwords
phonotactics: native words do not begin with r; old loans add a vowel (errege 'king', arrosa 'rose')
final clusters are sonorant or sibilant plus stop or affricate (beltz, hortz, bost)
stop plus stop sequences at word and morpheme boundaries are simplified, and a stop after a sibilant is voiceless
sequences of vowels across morpheme boundaries are changed in many dialects (etxea as [etʃia], [etʃie], [etʃea])

stress.type: weak accent fixed by position, with lexical exceptions; pitch accent in some dialects
stress.rule: In the central pattern that is widely used with the standard language the accent falls on the second syllable of the word or phrase, with a weaker prominence on the last syllable; words of two syllables have it on the first or the second syllable by variety; a minority of marked words (many loanwords, some compounds and plural forms) have it on the first syllable. The pronunciation rule of the Academy does not fix the accent.
stress.cues: mainly pitch, with some lengthening; intensity and vowel quality play little part

rhythm.notes: No rhythm measurements for Basque are cited here; the class follows the descriptive literature. Syllables differ little in duration and vowels keep their quality.

length.notes: No length contrast. Sequences of two like vowels arise where h is silent (zahar, mahai) and at morpheme boundaries; they are said as a long vowel or as two syllables.

intonation.declarative: each accentual phrase starts low and rises to the accented syllable; the phrase immediately before the verb is the focus position and carries the main prominence; the pitch range is compressed after it and the utterance ends low
intonation.yes_no_question: word order of the statement; in central and standard usage a rise at the end, or a question particle (al in Gipuzkoa, the suffix -a in the north) with a falling or level ending
intonation.wh_question: question word directly before the verb, with the main pitch peak; fall to a low ending
intonation.continuation: high or rising end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: in the central and standard pattern a rise to a peak on the accented second syllable; in Northern Bizkaian a high accented syllable followed by a sharp fall (H*+L)
intonation.notes: Elordieta and Hualde (2014). The best studied variety is Northern Bizkaian; statements about the standard language are less firm.

inventory.name: Northern Bizkaian accented word (dialect, not Standard Basque)
inventory.description: lexical accent on a fixed syllable (the penultimate in Lekeitio): low first syllable, high from the second syllable up to the accented one, then a sharp fall on the syllable after it (H*+L); each accent lowers the following peaks. The digits show the accented syllable and the one after it
inventory.duration: normal; the accent is carried by pitch, not by length

inventory.name: Northern Bizkaian unaccented word (dialect, not Standard Basque)
inventory.description: no lexical accent: low first syllable, then a high plateau that runs on into the next word without a fall; the word receives an accent on its last syllable only when it ends the phrase before the verb or is said alone. Most native words and singular forms belong here, so that singular and plural forms of a noun often differ by accent alone

inventory.name: Goizueta accent 1 (dialect, not Standard Basque)
inventory.description: stressed syllable (first or second of the word, lexically fixed) with rising or high pitch; schematic digits

inventory.name: Goizueta accent 2 (dialect, not Standard Basque)
inventory.description: stressed syllable (first or second of the word, lexically fixed) with falling or low pitch; schematic digits

sandhi: Northern Bizkaian: a sequence of unaccented words forms one accentual phrase with a single rise and a plateau; the peak after each accent is lowered (downstep)
tone.neutral_tone: none in the standard language; in Northern Bizkaian unaccented words carry only phrase-level pitch
tone.notes: Standard Basque and most dialects have a stress-like accent without lexical tone, so the type is given as none for the variety described. Two areas have lexical pitch accent. Northern Bizkaian (the coast from Getxo to Lekeitio, with Gernika) opposes accented and unaccented words, much like Tokyo Japanese (Hualde 1991, 1999; Hualde et al. 2002). Goizueta in Navarre has a four-way contrast: stress on the first or the second syllable, each with accent 1 or accent 2 (Hualde, Lujanbio and Torreira 2008; Hualde, Lujanbio and Zubiri 2010). The Chao digits are schematic, since no pitch values are cited here. eSpeak NG has no tone or pitch-accent phonemes for Basque.

problems: written j is always a voiced palatal stop [ɟ] (jan [ɟˈan], jakin, jende); the recommended standard value is [j] and the most common southern value is [x], which the rules offer only through a word flag
palatalisation of n and l after i applies to every word unless it is listed as an exception, so loanwords and learned words are changed too (zinema [s̻iɲˈemˌa], injineru [inɟˈiɲeɾˌu])

no pitch-accent model: every word gets the same positional accent, so the accent contrasts of the western dialects (singular versus plural forms) and the marked words with initial accent cannot be rendered
sibilants are not voiced before voiced consonants, and there is no option for the western merger of the two alveolar series
no tune set is selected, so the generic default tunes are used; the accent is realised with the generic stress mechanism, not as a pitch rise on the second syllable
the rules contain long lists of case endings as suffix rules, and the comments in the rule file mark several choices as uncertain (the value of j, lenition of d and g)
good: apical s [s̺] and laminal z [s̻] are separate phonemes with their own recordings, and so are the affricates ts [ts̺] and tz [ts̻]; tx and x are [tʃ] and [ʃ]
the palatal stops tt, dd and the palatals ñ, ll are present; tap and trill are distinguished
accent rule 15 puts the accent on the second syllable with a secondary prominence on the last, and the stress settings make all syllables nearly equal in length and loudness
approximant [β ð ɣ] between vowels; h is silent; devoicing after ez (ez dut [ˈes̻ tˈut], ez gara)

notes: The voice is marked as testing. It keeps the sibilant contrasts, which is the feature most easily lost when Basque is read with a Spanish voice. The main open questions are the value of j and the realisation of the accent by pitch.
